A recent social media post claims that getting a flu shot increases the risk of contracting COVID-19. This assertion has circulated online since the early days of the pandemic and continues to raise concerns among individuals seeking guidance on vaccine safety. To assess the validity of this claim, it is important to examine the scientific evidence, expert opinions, and relevant public health guidance.

The influenza vaccine, commonly referred to as the flu shot, is designed to protect against influenza viruses circulating during the flu season. COVID-19, on the other hand, is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, a different pathogen. Both illnesses can present with similar respiratory symptoms, but they are unrelated at a molecular level.

Early in the pandemic, some individuals speculated that receiving the flu vaccine might alter the immune system’s response to COVID-19 or make people more susceptible to infection. These concerns were fueled by misinterpretations of preliminary studies and misunderstandings about how vaccines work. However, the immune system’s response to vaccines is specific to the target pathogen; the flu vaccine prompts the body to build defenses against influenza viruses, not coronaviruses.

Major health organizations and immunologists have repeatedly addressed and refuted the idea that the flu shot increases COVID-19 risk. They emphasize that vaccines train the immune system to recognize and combat specific viruses, and there is no credible evidence that receiving the flu shot weakens the response to other viruses. In fact, during the pandemic, public health authorities recommended flu vaccinations to reduce the overall burden of respiratory illnesses and prevent strain on healthcare systems.

Some studies have explored whether vaccines could cause a phenomenon known as “viral interference,” where immunization against one virus may theoretically affect susceptibility to another. These studies have not produced consistent or conclusive findings, and the majority of research suggests no increased risk of COVID-19 as a result of receiving the flu vaccine. In some cases, vaccinated individuals appeared to have similar or lower rates of COVID-19 infection compared to those who did not get the flu shot.

It is also important to consider the broader public health context. Coinfection with influenza and COVID-19 can result in more severe illness, especially in vulnerable populations. By reducing the incidence of influenza through vaccination, the flu shot may actually help lessen the risk of dual infection and complications.

In summary, the claim that getting a flu shot increases the risk of COVID-19 is not supported by scientific evidence. The flu vaccine is safe, does not increase susceptibility to COVID-19, and remains an important tool for protecting public health during respiratory virus season. Individuals are encouraged to follow the advice of healthcare professionals and public health authorities regarding vaccination to safeguard themselves and their communities.

As the world continues to navigate the risks associated with COVID-19, a variety of home remedies and prevention strategies have surfaced on social media platforms. One claim that has circulated widely is the suggestion that rinsing your nose with saline solution could protect you from COVID-19. This article examines the basis of this claim, the current scientific evidence, and what health authorities recommend regarding nasal saline rinses and COVID-19 prevention.

Nasal saline rinses, sometimes called nasal irrigation, involve flushing the nasal passages with a saltwater solution. This practice has long been used to relieve symptoms of allergies, sinusitis, and upper respiratory tract infections by helping remove mucus, allergens, and irritants from the nose. Various devices, such as neti pots and squeeze bottles, are available for this purpose, and many people find the practice helpful for managing congestion and maintaining nasal hygiene.

The claim that saline rinsing could protect against COVID-19 appears to stem from the idea that mechanically washing the nasal passages might reduce the concentration of viruses, including SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19. Some proponents believe that this could lower the likelihood of infection if the virus is present in the nasal cavity.

However, the scientific evidence supporting nasal saline rinses as a protective measure against COVID-19 is limited. While nasal irrigation can help alleviate upper respiratory symptoms and may assist in clearing some pathogens from the nasal passages, there is no robust clinical evidence demonstrating that it can prevent infection with SARS-CoV-2. COVID-19 primarily spreads through respiratory droplets, and the virus can infect cells throughout the respiratory tract, not just in the nose. Simply rinsing the nose would not eliminate the virus from other areas, nor would it prevent exposure from inhaling airborne particles.

Major health organizations have not endorsed nasal saline rinses as a preventive strategy for COVID-19. Instead, they recommend well-established measures such as vaccination, wearing masks in crowded or enclosed spaces, practicing good hand hygiene, and maintaining physical distance from others where appropriate. These practices have been shown to significantly reduce the risk of infection and transmission of the virus.

It is also important to note that improper use of nasal irrigation devices or solutions can pose risks, including infections if non-sterile water is used or injury to the nasal passages. If individuals choose to use nasal rinses, they should follow medical advice on preparation and technique.

In summary, while nasal saline rinses may help relieve congestion and support nasal health, there is no conclusive evidence that the practice protects against COVID-19. The claim that rinsing your nose with saline solution could prevent COVID-19 is not supported by current scientific understanding or public health recommendations. Individuals concerned about COVID-19 protection should continue to follow proven preventive measures as advised by health authorities.

A recent social media post claims that smoking could protect individuals from COVID-19. This assertion has gained traction online, sparking discussions and raising questions about the relationship between tobacco use and susceptibility to the coronavirus. To evaluate this claim, it is important to examine the scientific evidence, consider the broader health implications of smoking, and understand how such statements may mislead the public.

The claim likely stems from early observations during the COVID-19 pandemic. Some initial studies noted a surprisingly low number of hospitalized COVID-19 patients who reported being current smokers. This led to speculation that nicotine or other components in tobacco might interfere with the virus’s ability to infect cells or modulate the immune response. However, these preliminary findings were quickly met with skepticism from the medical community, which cautioned against drawing conclusions from observational data that could be influenced by reporting bias, confounding factors, or incomplete patient histories.

Subsequent research has not supported the idea that smoking confers protection against COVID-19. In fact, the majority of studies indicate that smokers are at increased risk for severe outcomes if they contract the virus. Smoking damages lung tissue, impairs immune function, and increases susceptibility to respiratory infections. Individuals who smoke are more likely to develop complications such as pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and require mechanical ventilation if hospitalized with COVID-19. Additionally, chronic smoking is associated with comorbidities like cardiovascular disease, which are known risk factors for poor COVID-19 prognosis.

The notion that smoking might reduce the risk of COVID-19 infection is further undermined by the well-established harms of tobacco use. Smoking is a leading cause of preventable death worldwide, responsible for millions of deaths annually due to lung cancer, heart disease, stroke, and other serious conditions. Public health organizations universally advise against smoking and promote cessation as a means to improve overall health and reduce vulnerability to infections, including COVID-19.

It’s also important to recognize the potential dangers of spreading misinformation about smoking and COVID-19. Suggesting that smoking could be protective may encourage tobacco use, particularly among individuals seeking to reduce their risk of infection. This could have significant negative consequences for public health, as increased smoking rates would likely lead to more tobacco-related illnesses and deaths.

In summary, the claim that smoking could protect you from COVID-19 is not supported by credible scientific evidence. While some early observations prompted speculation, more rigorous research has shown that smoking is associated with worse outcomes among COVID-19 patients. Smoking remains a major health risk and should not be considered a means of preventing or mitigating the effects of COVID-19. The public is advised to rely on proven methods of protection, such as vaccination, mask-wearing, and maintaining good hand hygiene, rather than turning to tobacco use.

A recent social media post has been circulating, claiming that the “Amoxi” capsule, a medication made in the United States, is the only medicine that can completely cure COVID-19. This assertion has generated considerable attention and confusion online, especially as people seek reliable information about COVID-19 treatments. Fact-checking this claim involves examining the nature of “Amoxi,” its approved uses, and the current scientific consensus on COVID-19 therapies.

To begin, “Amoxi” is a commonly used shorthand for amoxicillin, an antibiotic in the penicillin family. Amoxicillin is widely prescribed for bacterial infections such as strep throat, ear infections, pneumonia, and sinusitis. It works by inhibiting the growth of bacteria, thereby helping the body fight off these specific infections. Amoxicillin is manufactured by several pharmaceutical companies, and while some production does occur in the United States, the drug is generic and produced internationally.

COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, is a viral infection—not a bacterial one. Antibiotics like amoxicillin are designed to target bacteria, not viruses. Therefore, amoxicillin has no direct effect on the virus responsible for COVID-19. In some cases, doctors may prescribe antibiotics to COVID-19 patients who develop secondary bacterial infections as a complication, but these medicines do not treat the underlying viral infection itself.

The claim that “Amoxi” is the only medicine that can “completely cure” COVID-19 is not supported by medical evidence or public health guidelines. No reputable health authority, such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration or the World Health Organization, endorses amoxicillin (or any antibiotic) as a cure for COVID-19. The treatment for COVID-19 typically involves antiviral medications, supportive care, and, in severe cases, interventions such as oxygen therapy or steroids. Several antiviral drugs, such as remdesivir and nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid), have received emergency use authorization or approval for use in certain patients with COVID-19, but none are described as a “complete cure.”

Furthermore, the idea that any single medication—antibiotic or otherwise—can universally “cure” COVID-19 is misleading. The course and severity of COVID-19 can vary widely depending on factors like age, underlying health conditions, and vaccination status. While many people recover from COVID-19 with or without medication, some experience prolonged symptoms or complications, and some require hospitalization.

In summary, the claim that the “Amoxi” capsule is the only medicine that can completely cure COVID-19 is false. Amoxicillin does not treat viral infections like COVID-19, and no single medication is recognized as a cure for the disease. It is essential to rely on guidance from medical professionals and health authorities for accurate information on COVID-19 prevention and treatment. Sharing unsubstantiated claims about treatments can be dangerous, especially during an ongoing global pandemic.

Claims that drugs traditionally used against malaria, specifically hydroxychloroquine, along with the antibiotic azithromycin, can cure COVID-19 have circulated widely since the early days of the pandemic. The assertion has sparked intense debate, influenced treatment approaches, and led to confusion among the public. This article examines the origins of this claim, the scientific evidence available, and the current consensus among medical experts.

Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial drug that has also been used to treat autoimmune disorders such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. Azithromycin is an antibiotic commonly prescribed for bacterial infections. Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, both drugs gained attention when preliminary laboratory studies suggested they might inhibit the replication of SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, in cell cultures. This laboratory evidence, combined with small-scale clinical studies, led some to believe that these drugs could be effective treatments for COVID-19.

Support for the use of hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin was further fueled by anecdotal reports and high-profile endorsements. However, it is important to distinguish between laboratory findings and results from rigorous clinical trials involving actual patients. Initial small studies were either inconclusive or methodologically flawed, lacking control groups or sufficient sample sizes. Despite this, some governments and individuals began stockpiling the drugs, and the medications saw a surge in off-label use.

As the pandemic progressed, larger and more comprehensive clinical trials were conducted to assess the safety and effectiveness of hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin in treating COVID-19. These trials consistently found that hydroxychloroquine, used alone or in combination with azithromycin, did not reduce mortality or speed up recovery in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Furthermore, some studies indicated that using the drugs together could increase the risk of serious side effects, particularly heart rhythm problems.

Major health organizations, including the World Health Organization and national regulatory agencies, reviewed the available evidence and updated their recommendations. They concluded that hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin should not be used to treat COVID-19 outside of clinical trials. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, for example, revoked its emergency use authorization for hydroxychloroquine in COVID-19 treatment due to concerns about both efficacy and safety.

While research is ongoing into treatments for COVID-19, the current scientific consensus is clear: hydroxychloroquine, azithromycin, and their combination do not cure COVID-19. The most effective strategies for managing the disease remain supportive care and, in severe cases, the use of therapies with proven benefit, such as corticosteroids for certain hospitalized patients. Vaccination remains the primary tool for preventing severe illness and death from COVID-19.

In summary, while the hope for a simple pharmaceutical cure for COVID-19 was understandable, the claim that antimalarial drugs like hydroxychloroquine and antibiotics like azithromycin can cure COVID-19 is not supported by scientific evidence. Public health recommendations are based on the best available data, and currently, these drugs are not considered effective or safe treatments for COVID-19.

In recent days, a social media post has circulated widely, claiming that the World Health Organization (WHO) has confirmed COVID-19 as airborne. This statement has generated renewed public interest and some confusion over how SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, actually spreads. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine the context of the WHO’s guidance, the evolving scientific understanding of COVID-19 transmission, and what “airborne” means in this context.

At the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020, public health authorities, including the WHO, stated that the primary mode of transmission for the novel coronavirus was through respiratory droplets. These droplets, produced when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or speaks, are relatively large and tend to fall to the ground or nearby surfaces within a short distance. This guidance shaped recommendations on physical distancing and mask-wearing.

However, as the pandemic progressed, scientists began to observe instances where traditional droplet-based transmission did not fully explain the spread of the virus, particularly in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces. In response to growing evidence from aerosol scientists and epidemiologists, there was increasing discussion about the role of smaller particles—known as aerosols—in COVID-19 transmission. Aerosols can remain suspended in the air for extended periods and travel longer distances, especially indoors.

Acknowledging this evidence, in mid-2020, the WHO updated its language to recognize the possibility of airborne transmission in specific circumstances, such as during medical procedures that generate aerosols. Over time, the organization further revised its guidance, stating that COVID-19 can spread through both droplets and aerosols, especially in indoor or crowded settings with inadequate ventilation.

By 2021, the WHO and other public health agencies began to emphasize the importance of airborne precautions, recommending improved indoor ventilation, air filtration, and high-quality masks, especially in situations where people gather indoors for prolonged periods. The current consensus among experts, reflected in WHO’s guidance, is that SARS-CoV-2 can indeed spread via aerosols in the air, and that airborne transmission plays a significant role in the spread of COVID-19, particularly under certain conditions.

Therefore, the claim that “WHO confirmed COVID-19 as airborne” is largely accurate, though it lacks some nuance. The WHO’s position has evolved over time as scientific understanding improved. Today, the organization recognizes airborne transmission as a significant pathway for the virus, especially indoors. However, the term “airborne” can mean different things in different scientific and medical contexts. For COVID-19, it refers to the potential for smaller respiratory particles to remain suspended and travel in the air, not just the traditional sense used for diseases like measles.

In summary, the social media post reflects the current scientific consensus and WHO guidance: COVID-19 can be transmitted through the air, especially in poorly ventilated spaces. As a result, preventive measures now include improving ventilation, using effective masks, and avoiding crowded indoor environments, in addition to traditional hygiene measures.

Need liitmed, mis tekivad, kui nakatunud inimene hingab, kõhutab või räägitakse, on suured ja liiguvad tõenäoliselt väga lühikese kaasaegu pinnale või lähedale olevate pindadele. See juhendus mõjutas soovitusi füüsilise kauguse ja maski kasutamise kohta.

Kuid pandeemias arendunud ajal algasid teadlased märkima näiteid, kus traditsioonilise liitme põhjustatud levimine ei selgitanud täielikult viiruse levimist, eriti sulgudes, kus õhukäänd on halvendatud. Reaalsete tõendite alusel, mis on toonud esile aerosoolte teadlased ja epidemioloogid, suurenes sümptomeid, et väiksemate osakeste – neid nimetatakse aerosoolideks – rolli COVI-19 levimises. Aerosoolid võivad jääda õhukäändusse mitte väga lühikese ajaga ja liiguda kaugemale, eriti sisekäändes.

Täname seda tõendit, 2020. aasta keskel uuendas WHO oma keele, et tõhusust õhukäändu põhjustatud levimist oluliseks eriti meditsiiniliste protseduuride juures, mis toovad esile aerosoolid. Aja jooksul uuendas organisatsioon oma juhendust, ütlema, et COVI-19 levib nii liitme kui ka aerosoolide kaudu, eriti sisekäändes või ülekoormatud kohtades, kus õhukäänd on ebapiisav.

2021. aastal alustas WHO ja teised tervishoiuorganisatsioonid paindlikkuse tõhususe määratlemist, soovitades sisekäändes paremat õhukäändu, õhukäändu filtreerimist ja kõrge kvaliteediga maskide kasutamist eriti oluliste kohtade puhul, kus inimesed kogunevad sisekäändes pikka aja jooksul. Tänapäeval teadlaste üleliikumine, mida peegeldab WHO juhendus, on see, et SARS-CoV-2 saab tõesti levida õhukäändusse, ja et õhukäändu levimine mängib olulist rolli COVI-19 levimises, eriti mõne tingimuse all.

Seega väide, et "WHO kinnitas COVI-19 õhukäänduvaks", on üldiselt tõhus, kuid see ei kattu täielikult. WHO seisukoht on arendunud ajal, kui teaduskäsitlus on arendunud. Tänapäeval tunnustab organisatsioon õhukäändu levimise oluliseks viiruse levimise viisiks, eriti sisekäändes. Kuid sõna "õhukäänduv" võib tähendada erinevalt teaduslikul ja meditsiinilisel kontekstis. COVI-19 puhul viitab see väikeseid hingamisliitmeid, mis jäävad õhukäändusse ja liiguvad õhukäändusse, mitte ainult traditsioonilise tähendusega, nagu on näha mees, kus õhukäänd on põhjustatud.

Kokkuvõttes, ülemaailmne kogukond peegeldab tänapäevast teaduskäsitlust ja WHO juhendust: COVI-19 saab levida õhukäändus, eriti halvendatud õhukäändusse. Seetõttu on eelarvamused nüüd kaasatud õhukäändu parandamiseks, efektiivse maski kasutamiseks ja kogunemise vältimiseks sisekäändes, lisaks traditsioonilise higihoolduse meetoditele.

article_content:
A popular claim circulating on social media suggests that you can test the quality of a reusable mask by wearing it and attempting to blow out a lighter flame. According to the post, if you are unable to extinguish the flame, the mask is considered effective; if you can, the mask is ineffective. This simple “lighter test” has been widely shared as a quick method for evaluating the filtration capability of cloth and reusable face masks, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic when mask usage became common worldwide.

To assess the validity of this claim, it is important to understand how masks work and what standards are used to evaluate their performance. Masks—whether disposable or reusable—are primarily designed to filter out respiratory droplets and, in some cases, smaller airborne particles. Their effectiveness depends on multiple factors, including the type of fabric, the number of layers, the fit on the face, and the filtration efficiency of the material.

The lighter test is based on the idea that if air passes through the mask forcefully enough to blow out a flame, then droplets and particles could also pass through, making the mask ineffective. In practice, however, this method oversimplifies the science behind mask filtration. The ability to blow out a lighter is influenced not only by the mask’s filtration capacity but also by the mask’s fit, the force of the breath, and the size of the particles being blocked. A mask might prevent large droplets from escaping but still allow enough airflow to extinguish a flame, or vice versa.

Moreover, laboratory testing of masks involves specialized equipment to measure the percentage of particles filtered at specific sizes, such as 0.3 microns, and at controlled airflow rates. These tests are far more precise than a home “lighter test” and consider factors like breathability and filtration under realistic conditions. The lighter test does not account for these important variables and provides no quantitative measurement of mask efficiency.

Health experts warn against relying on unscientific methods such as the lighter test to judge mask quality. A mask’s inability to blow out a flame does not necessarily mean it meets established standards for filtration or fit. Conversely, a mask that allows you to extinguish a lighter may still provide some level of protection, depending on its materials and construction.

In conclusion, while the lighter test is easy to perform and may give a rough indication of how much airflow a mask allows, it is not a reliable or scientifically valid method for determining the quality or effectiveness of a reusable mask. For maximum protection, individuals should look for masks made from multiple layers of tightly woven fabric, ensure a snug fit over the nose and mouth, and, when possible, use masks that meet recognized standards for filtration efficiency. Relying solely on the lighter test may provide a false sense of security and should not replace proper guidelines for mask selection and use.

ସ୍ୱାସ୍ଥ୍ୟ ବିଶାରଦମାନେ ଲାଇଟର ପରୀକ୍ଷା ପରି ଅନ୍ୟାନ୍ୟ ଅନୁପାତିକ ପଦ୍ଧତିରେ ମାସ୍କ ଗୁଣବତ୍ତା ନିର୍ଣ୍ଣୟ କରିବାରେ ନିର୍ଭର କରିବା ବିରୋଧରେ ଚେତାବନୀ ଦେଇଛନ୍ତି। ଏକ ମାସ୍କ ଆଗୁରୁ ନିର୍ମୂଳ କରିବାର ଅକ୍ଷମତା ମାନକରେ ଫିଲ୍ଟ୍ରେସନ ବା ଫିଟିଂ ପାଇଁ ପ୍ରମାଣିତ ନଥିବା ମଧ୍ୟ ହୋଇପାରେ। ଅନ୍ୟପକ୍ଷରେ, ଏକ ମାସ୍କ ଯେଉଁଥିରେ ଆଗୁରୁ ନିର୍ମୂଳ କରିବାର କ୍ଷମତା ରହିଛି, ତେବେ ମାତ୍ର କେତେକ ପ୍ରକାରର ରକ୍ଷା ପ୍ରଦାନ କରିପାରିବ, ଯାହା ଏହାର ପ୍ରକାର ଏବଂ ନିର୍ମାଣ ଉପରେ ନିର୍ଭର କରିଥାଏ।

ଶେଷରେ, ଯଦିଓ ଲାଇଟର ପରୀକ୍ଷା କରିବା ଅଧିକ ପ୍ରାଚୁର୍ଯ୍ୟ ଏବଂ ମାସ୍କ କେତେ ବାତାହଳ ପ୍ରଦାନ କରିଥାଏ ଏହାର ପ୍ରାଥମିକ ଅଭିମାନ ପ୍ରଦାନ କରିପାରିବ, ଏହା ପୁନଃବ୍ୟବହାର କରିଥାଏନ୍ଟ ମାସ୍କର ଗୁଣବତ୍ତା ବା କ୍ଷମତା ନିର୍ଣ୍ଣୟ କରିବା ପାଇଁ ପ୍ରଭାବଶାଳୀ ବା ବିଜ୍ଞାନପୂର୍ଣ୍ଣ ପଦ୍ଧତି ନୁହେଁ। ପ୍ରାପ୍ୟ ରକ୍ଷା ପାଇଁ, ବ୍ୟକ୍ତିମାନେ ବହୁତ ଲୟର୍ରେ ଘନଭାବରେ ବ୍ୟବହୃତ କପାଳରୁ ତିଆରି ମାସ୍କ ଖୋଜିବା ଉଚିତ, ମୁଖ ଏବଂ ଚାହାରେ ଠିକ୍ ଫିଟିଂ ନିଶ୍ଚିତ କରନ୍ତୁ ଏବଂ ଯଦି ସମ୍ଭବ ହୋଇଥାଏ, ଫିଲ୍ଟ୍ରେସନ କ୍ଷମତା ପ୍ରମାଣିତ ମାସ୍କ ବ୍ୟବହାର କରନ୍ତୁ। କେବଳ ଲାଇଟର ପରୀକ୍ଷାରେ ନିର୍ଭର କରିବା ଭ୍ରମାତ୍ମକ ଅପରିଚିତ ଅନୁଭୂତିର ଅନୁଭବ ପ୍ରଦାନ କରିପାରେ ଏବଂ ମାସ୍କ ବିଚାର ଏବଂ ବ୍ୟବହାର ପାଇଁ ପ୍ରମାଣିତ ପଦ୍ଧତିର ପରିବର୍ତ୍ତେ ହୋଇପାରିବ।

As the world continues to navigate the ongoing presence of COVID-19, understanding the symptoms associated with the virus remains essential for both public health and individual safety. A recent social media post claims, "A runny nose is not a COVID-19 symptom." This statement has gained traction online, potentially leading to misconceptions about how COVID-19 presents itself and how individuals should respond to their symptoms. In this fact-check, we examine whether a runny nose is truly not a symptom of COVID-19 and provide context on how the virus manifests.

COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, was first identified in late 2019. Since then, health organizations around the world have tracked and updated information about its symptoms as new variants have emerged and more data has become available. In the early months of the pandemic, the most frequently reported symptoms included fever, dry cough, and fatigue. These "classic" symptoms set COVID-19 apart from other respiratory illnesses like the common cold and seasonal flu, which often present with a runny nose and sneezing.

However, as the virus spread and new variants developed, the symptom profile broadened. Reports of sore throat, headache, muscle aches, and loss of taste or smell became prominent. Notably, several studies and health authority updates have noted that a runny nose can also occur in people infected with COVID-19, particularly as new variants have circulated.

A runny nose, medically known as rhinorrhea, became more commonly reported with the emergence of the Omicron variant and its subvariants. With these variants, the symptom profile shifted to include more upper respiratory tract symptoms, closely resembling those of a common cold. People with Omicron infections have frequently reported symptoms such as sore throat, sneezing, and runny nose, in addition to the more established signs of COVID-19.

Nonetheless, while a runny nose can be a symptom of COVID-19, it is not exclusive to the virus. Many other illnesses, such as the common cold, seasonal allergies, and influenza, can cause a runny nose. This overlap can make it challenging for individuals to determine the cause of their symptoms without testing. Importantly, public health experts advise that anyone experiencing new respiratory symptoms—including a runny nose—should consider the possibility of COVID-19, especially in the context of exposure or rising community transmission rates.

In summary, the claim that "a runny nose is not a COVID-19 symptom" is inaccurate. While a runny nose may not have been a hallmark symptom at the onset of the pandemic, it is now recognized as one of the possible symptoms, particularly with certain variants. As knowledge about COVID-19 continues to evolve, it is important for the public to stay informed through credible sources and to seek testing when experiencing symptoms that could be related to COVID-19. Misconceptions about symptoms can lead to underestimating the risk of infection and hinder efforts to control the spread of the virus.

Et nyligt sociale medierindlæg påstår, "En næseflue er ikke et symptom på COVID-19." I denne faktacheck undersøger vi, om en næseflue virkelig ikke er et symptom på COVID-19, og giver kontekst om, hvordan viruset udtrykker sig.

Efterfølgende har sundhedsorganisationer i hele verden sporet og opdateret information om symptomerne, som nye varianters opdagede og mere data blev tilgængeligt. I de første måneder af pandemien var de mest frekvent rapporterede symptomer feber, tør røg, og træthed. Disse "klassiske" symptomer skilte COVID-19 fra andre luftvejsinfektioner som den almindelige rhinokonjunktivitis og sæsonale gripe, som ofte præsenterer sig med en næseflue og næsefølelse.

Bemærkelsesværdig var, at flere studier og opdateringer fra sundhedsmyndigheder har påpeget, at en næseflue kan opstå hos personer, der er inficerede med COVID-19, især som nye varianters omkringkomst.

En næseflue, medicinsk kendt som rhinorrhea, blev mere ofte rapporteret med opståelsen af Omicron-varianten og dens undervarianter. Med disse varianters fremtrædelse forandret sig symptomprofilen til at inkludere flere luftvejsrelaterede symptomer, som er tæt på dem, der typisk optræder ved den almindelige rhinokonjunktivitis. Dog, selvom en næseflue kan være et symptom på COVID-19, er det ikke eksklusivt for viruset. Mange andre sygdomme, som den almindelige rhinokonjunktivitis, sæsonale allergier og influensa, kan forårsage en næseflue. Denne overlægning kan gøre det svært for individer at bestemme årsagen til deres symptomer uden test. Vigtigt er det, at offentlige sundhedseksperter anbefaler, at enhver, der oplever nye luftvejs-symptomer – herunder en næseflue – bør overveje muligheden for COVID-19, især i konteksten af eksponering eller stigende samfundstransmission.

Samlet set er påstanden, at "en næseflue ikke er et symptom på COVID-19", fejlbevidst. Selvom en næseflue måske ikke har været et prægnant symptom i starten af pandemien, er den nu genkendt som et af de mulige symptomer, især med visse varianters fremtrædelse. Da viden om COVID-19 fortsætter med at udvikle sig, er det vigtigt for offentligheden at holde sig informeret gennem pålidelige kilder og at søge test, når man oplever symptomer, der kan være relateret til COVID-19. Fejlagtige forestillinger om symptomer kan føre til en underestimering af risikoen for infektion og hindre anstrengelserne for at kontrollere spredningen af viruset.

A social media post circulating widely claims that drinking a lot of water and gargling with warm water mixed with salt or vinegar can eliminate “the virus.” This advice, often shared in the context of viral respiratory infections such as COVID-19, suggests that these simple home remedies can prevent or cure infection by eliminating the virus from the throat or body. We examined this claim to determine its accuracy and to provide readers with evidence-based guidance.

The post’s core assertion revolves around two main ideas: first, that drinking a large quantity of water helps to protect against viral infections, and second, that gargling with saltwater or vinegar effectively eliminates the virus from the throat, thereby preventing illness.

Drinking adequate amounts of water is universally recognized as important for general health. Staying hydrated supports many bodily functions, including the immune system. However, the claim that drinking excessive amounts of water can “eliminate the virus” is misleading. Once a virus, such as the one responsible for COVID-19, enters the body, it infects cells in the respiratory tract and begins replicating. Simply drinking water will not wash the virus out of the body or prevent it from establishing an infection. While it is true that drinking water can soothe the throat and may help with symptoms of mild respiratory illness, it does not serve as a cure or a preventive measure against viral infection.

The second part of the claim focuses on the use of saltwater or vinegar gargles. Gargling with warm saltwater has long been recommended as a home remedy for soothing sore throats and reducing discomfort caused by common colds or minor throat irritations. Saltwater can temporarily reduce inflammation and may help flush out some mucus, but it does not destroy viruses or prevent their entry into cells. There is no scientific evidence that gargling with saltwater can eliminate viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

Similarly, vinegar is known for its antibacterial properties, but using vinegar as a gargle can irritate the sensitive tissues in the mouth and throat, and it has not been proven to kill viruses in the human respiratory tract. Health authorities do not recommend vinegar gargles as a treatment or preventive measure for viral infections.

In summary, while staying hydrated and gargling with warm saltwater may provide symptomatic relief for sore throats, these measures do not eliminate viruses from the body or serve as effective prevention against viral illnesses. The most reliable ways to protect oneself from respiratory viruses include vaccination, practicing good hand hygiene, wearing masks in crowded settings, and following public health guidelines. People should be cautious about unproven home remedies and seek information from trusted medical sources when making decisions about their health.

Ievērojams sociālajā tīklā plātīgāk izplatīts ziņojums apgalvo, ka lielu ūdens daudzumu dzert un sāļu vai vīnu maisījumu ar siltu ūdeni var iznīcināt „vīrusu“. Šis padoms, bieži šķiroties vīrusu izraisītās elpošanas ceļu infekcijām, piemēram, koronavīrusa infekcijai (COVID-19), ieteicās, ka šie vienkāršie mājās izmantotie līdzekļi var novērst vai iznīcināt infekciju, iznīcinot vīrusu gļotāju vai ķermeņa iekšienē. Mēs pārbaudījām šo apgalvojumu, lai noteiktu tās patiesumu un piedāvātu lasītājiem balstītu uzskatu vadību.

Ziņojuma galvenais apgalvojums apvieno divus galvenos punktus: pirmkārt, ka lielu ūdens daudzumu dzert palīdz aizsargāt no vīrusu infekcijām, un otrkārt, ka sālīta vai vīna ar siltu ūdeni izvārīšana efektīvi iznīcina vīrusu gļotājā, tādēļ novēršot slimību.

Pietiekams ūdens daudzums tiek vispārpieņemts kā svarīgs vispārējam veselības nodrošināšanai. Hidratācija atbalsta daudzas ķermeņa funkcijas, tostarp imūnsistēmas darbību. Tomēr apgalvojums, ka pārmērīgs ūdens dzēriens var „iznīcināt vīrusu“, ir nepareizs. Reiz, kad vīruss, piemēram, koronavīruss (SARS-CoV-2), ienāk ķermenī, tas inficē elpošanas ceļu šūnas un sāk replikēties. Pārmērīgs ūdens dzēriens nevar izvārīt vīrusu no ķermeņa vai novērst tā infekcijas izveidošanos. Tomēr ir patiesība, ka ūdens dzēriens var mierināt gļotāju un var palīdzēt arī simptomiem no mazām elpošanas ceļu slimībām, taču tas nav ārstējums vai aizsardzības līdzeklis pret vīrusu infekcijām.

Otrās daļas apgalvojums koncentrējas uz sālīta vai vīna ar siltu ūdeni izvārīšanas izmantošanu. Siltā sālīta ūdens izvārīšana ir ilgstoši ieteikta mājās izmantotā līdzekļa, lai mierinātu sāpīgu gļotāju un samazinātu neērtības, kas rodas no parastās gripas vai mazām gļotāju traucējumiem. Sālsūdens var ilgstoši samazināt iekaisumu un var palīdzēt izvārīt dažus mēslus, taču tā neiznīcina vīrusus vai novērš to iekļūšanu šūnās. Nav zinātniski pierādīts, ka sālīta ūdens izvārīšana var iznīcināt vīrusus, piemēram, SARS-CoV-2, kas izraisa koronavīrusu infekciju.

Līdzīgi, vīns ir pazīstams ar antibakteriālām īpašībām, taču vīna izvārīšana var izraisīt neaizsargātu ķermeņa vai gļotāju audu iedegumu, un tā nav pierādīta, ka tā var iznīcināt vīrusus cilvēka elpošanas ceļos. Veselības aģentūras neietekmē vīna izvārīšanas izmantošanu kā ārstējumu vai aizsardzības līdzekli pret vīrusu infekcijām.

Kopsavilkumā, lai gan dzert pietiekami daudz ūdens un izvārīšana ar siltu sālītu ūdeni var sniegt simptomu atvieglotību sāpīgām gļotājām, šie līdzekļi neiznīcina vīrusus no ķermeņa vai nevar izmantot kā efektīvu aizsardzības līdzekli pret vīrusu slimībām. article_content:
A claim recently circulating on social media asserts that onions can be applied to cure COVID-19, suggesting they were similarly effective against the Spanish flu in 1918. This statement has generated considerable interest, especially among those seeking natural remedies for viral infections. However, a thorough review of historical records, scientific data, and expert opinions reveals that this claim is not supported by credible evidence.

To understand the origins of this belief, it is important to look back at the 1918 influenza pandemic, widely known as the Spanish flu. During that time, medical knowledge was limited, and many folk remedies were promoted in the absence of effective treatments. Onions, along with other home remedies such as garlic, mustard plasters, and herbal concoctions, were often used in an attempt to ward off illness. Some anecdotal stories from that era described families hanging onions in their homes or placing sliced onions near sick patients, believing that the vegetable could absorb viruses or bacteria from the air. However, these practices were not based on scientific research; rather, they reflected the limited understanding of disease transmission and prevention at the time.

Fast forward to the present day and the global COVID-19 pandemic, and similar claims about onions have resurfaced online. Proponents suggest that applying or consuming onions can cure or prevent COVID-19, drawing parallels to the Spanish flu era. However, there is no scientific evidence to support the idea that onions have antiviral properties effective against the novel coronavirus. COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, and its prevention and treatment have been thoroughly studied by the global medical community. Approved vaccines, antiviral medications, and public health measures remain the only proven methods to reduce transmission and severity of the disease.

The belief that onions can absorb viruses or cure viral infections is a persistent myth. While onions are a nutritious food and contain some compounds that may have mild antimicrobial effects, these properties are not significant enough to offer protection against powerful viruses such as influenza or SARS-CoV-2. No clinical studies have demonstrated that applying onions to the skin or placing them in a room can treat or prevent respiratory viruses. In fact, relying on such unproven remedies may delay individuals from seeking appropriate medical care or adhering to public health recommendations.

In summary, the core claim that onions could be applied to cure COVID-19, as they allegedly did during the Spanish flu of 1918, is not supported by historical records or scientific evidence. While onions are a healthy addition to the diet, they should not be considered a substitute for proven preventive and therapeutic measures against COVID-19 or any other serious viral infection. Misinformation about home remedies can be harmful, and it is important to consult medical professionals and trusted sources for guidance on disease prevention and treatment.

A social media post has recently circulated suggesting that consuming herbs, specifically "curmin" (which appears to be a misspelling or variant of "curcumin," a compound found in turmeric), as practiced by people in India, will keep individuals safe from COVID-19. This claim aligns with a broader trend of attributing disease prevention or cure to certain foods or natural remedies, particularly during global health crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to provide context about both COVID-19 and the role of herbal supplements in disease prevention. COVID-19 is a respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which emerged in late 2019 and rapidly spread worldwide. Public health measures such as vaccines, mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and social distancing have been scientifically validated as effective ways to reduce transmission and severity of the disease.

Turmeric, a common spice in Indian cuisine, contains curcumin, which has been studied for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Traditional systems of medicine in India, such as Ayurveda, have long promoted the use of herbs, including turmeric, for general health and wellness. During the pandemic, there was increased interest in whether such traditional remedies might offer protection against COVID-19.

However, the assertion that eating herbs or curcumin can make someone "safe" from COVID-19 is not supported by scientific evidence. While curcumin has shown some promise in laboratory studies for its anti-inflammatory effects, there is no robust clinical data demonstrating that it prevents infection with the coronavirus or significantly reduces the risk of severe illness. No major health organizations have endorsed herbal supplements as a substitute for vaccination or other approved preventive measures.

Furthermore, the post implies that people in India, presumably due to their consumption of herbs and curcumin, are safe from COVID-19. This is misleading. India experienced several severe waves of COVID-19, with high rates of infection, hospitalization, and mortality, despite widespread use of turmeric and other traditional remedies. These events underscore that nutritional habits alone are not sufficient protection against a highly contagious virus.

It is possible that maintaining a healthy diet, including the use of herbs and spices, could contribute to overall well-being and immune system support. However, such practices should not be regarded as a primary defense against COVID-19. The most effective strategies for preventing COVID-19 remain vaccination, adherence to public health guidelines, and timely medical intervention.

In summary, while the consumption of herbs like curcumin is part of traditional Indian diets and may have general health benefits, there is no scientific basis for the claim that it will make individuals safe from COVID-19. Relying solely on dietary supplements or herbs instead of proven preventive measures places individuals at increased risk. It is crucial to look to established medical advice rather than unsubstantiated social media claims when it comes to COVID-19 prevention.

Echter, hierdie praktyke moet nie as 'n primêre verdediging teen COVID-19 beskou word nie. A recent social media post claims that “Zinc Lozenges was proved a protection to COVID-19.” This assertion suggests that using zinc lozenges is a proven method to prevent or protect against COVID-19 infection. Fact-checking such health-related claims is crucial, especially in the context of an ongoing global pandemic.

To evaluate this claim, it is important to provide some background on zinc and its purported antiviral properties. Zinc is an essential mineral that plays a vital role in immune function. Over the years, zinc lozenges have gained popularity as a potential remedy for the common cold, with some studies suggesting that zinc may help reduce the duration or severity of cold symptoms when taken soon after symptom onset. The rationale behind this is that zinc can impede the replication of certain viruses in the upper respiratory tract.

With the emergence of COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, there has been widespread interest in potential interventions—both pharmaceutical and over-the-counter—that might prevent infection or lessen disease severity. Early in the pandemic, discussions about zinc supplements and lozenges circulated in the media and on social networks, fueled by the mineral's established role in immune support and some laboratory studies suggesting that zinc might inhibit coronavirus replication in cell cultures.

However, translating laboratory findings or results from studies on the common cold to the specific context of COVID-19 requires robust clinical evidence. To date, scientific research has not conclusively proven that zinc lozenges protect against COVID-19. While some small studies have explored zinc supplementation for hospitalized COVID-19 patients, the results have been mixed, and these studies mostly addressed the use of oral or intravenous zinc as a treatment, not as a preventative lozenge.

Major health organizations have not endorsed zinc lozenges as a preventative or therapeutic measure for COVID-19. Current recommendations stress the importance of vaccines, mask-wearing in high-risk settings, and other public health measures as the primary forms of protection. Zinc supplementation is generally only recommended for individuals who have a diagnosed deficiency, as excessive zinc intake can lead to adverse effects, including nausea, diarrhea, and interference with the absorption of other essential minerals.

In summary, while zinc is important for immune health and may play a role in combating certain viral infections, there is no robust clinical evidence that zinc lozenges have been "proved" to protect against COVID-19. The scientific consensus does not support the claim made in the social media post. Individuals should rely on evidence-based recommendations and consult healthcare professionals before taking supplements for COVID-19 prevention or treatment. As always, it is important to be cautious about health claims circulating on social media that are not backed by strong scientific evidence.

Verifikimi i këtyre afirimeve shëndetësore është i rëndësishëm, të veçantë në kontekstin e pandemisë globale të vazhdueshme.

Për të vlerësuar këtë afirim, është e rëndësishme të ofrohet një kontekst i mëparshëm për zinkun dhe vetëso e tij antivirale. Zinku është një minerale e rëndësishme që luan një rol të rëndësishëm në funksionin e sistemit imunitar. Në vite të kaluara, lozengët e zincut janë marrë në shqyrtim si mundësi e potenciale për të trajtuar gripin, me disa studime që thonë se zinku mund të ndihmojë në mësime të shpejtë ose të rrëshqitur të simptomave të gripit nëse merret shpejt pas fillimit të simptomave. Razoni për këtë është se zinku mund të ndikojë në replikimin e disa virusëve në traktin e sipërm të frymëmarrjes.

Me emergjenin e koronavirusit, shkaktuar nga virusi SARS-CoV-2, ka qënë interes në mundësi të mundshme të ndryshme – të shëndetësishme dhe të disponueshme – që mund të ndaloni infeksionin ose të lehtësojnë rëndësinë e së së shpejtit. Më herët në pandeminë, diskutime për suplementet e zinkut dhe lozengët e tij janë shpërndarë në mediat dhe në sotiale, duke përfshirë rolin e mineraleve të përcaktuar në mbrojtjen e sistemit imunitar dhe disa studime laboratorike që sugjeronin se zinku mund të ndalonte replikimin e koronavirusit në kulturat e qelizave.

Por, translacioni i rezultateve të laboratorit ose të studimeve të gripit në kontekstin të veçantë të koronavirusit të ka nevojë për evidencë klinike të tërësishme. Në këtë kohë, studimet shkencimore nuk kanë konfirmuar të plotë se lozengët e zincut mbrojten nga koronavirusi. Në të kaluarën, disa studime të vogla kanë shqyrtuar suplementimin e zinkut për pacientët e hospitalizuar me koronavirus, por rezultatet janë të moshuar, dhe këto studime janë shumë të adresuan përdorimin e zinkut të shpërndarë apo intravenoz si trajtim, jo si lozengë preventiv.

Organizatat shëndetësore të rëndësishme nuk janë të mbrojtura në lozengët e zincut si trajtim ose mbrojtje preventivë për koronavirusin. Recomandimet aktuale theksojnë rëndësinë e vakcinave, mbrojtjes me maske në situacionet e rrezikshme, dhe të tjerat masë të shëndetësisë publike si formë kryesore të mbrojtjes. Suplementimi me zink është në përgjithësi të rekomanduar vetëm për individët që janë diagnostikuar me deficite, sepse përdorimi i shumë zinkut mund të shkaktojë efekte negative, si të vështira, të kërcënomës, dhe ndikimin në mbrojtjen e mineraleve të tjera të rëndësishme.

Në përfundim, pëndësishme zinku në shëndetin e sistemit imunitar dhe mund të lëndë të rëndësishme në ndalimin e disa infeksioneve virale, nuk ka evidencë klinike të tërësishme se lozengët e zincut janë “provuar” të mbrojten nga koronavirusi. Konsensusi shkencor nuk mbrojtë afirimin e bërë në postimin e sotiale. Individët duhet të përkthejnë në rekomandimet e bazuara në fakte dhe të konsultojnë profesionistët e shëndetësisë përpara se të merren suplementë për ndalimin apo trajtimin e koronavirusit. Si gjithë kohë, është e rëndësishme të jeni kujdes në afirimet shëndetësore që shpërndahen në sotiale që nuk janë të mbrojtura nga evidencë shkencimore të tërësishme.

The emergence of COVID-19 in late 2019 brought about global concern not only due to its rapid transmission but also because of its potential long-term health impacts. Recently, a social media post has circulated, claiming that Chinese experts warn about a “scar in the lungs” left by COVID-19, and that this effect is more severe than that seen with SARS 17 years ago. This article examines the validity of this claim, providing context and analysis based on available evidence and expert opinions.

To understand the claim, it is important first to recognize what is meant by a “scar in the lungs.” Lung scarring, medically referred to as pulmonary fibrosis, occurs when lung tissue becomes damaged and scarred, leading to chronic breathing difficulties and reduced oxygen exchange. Both SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome), which emerged in 2002-2003, and COVID-19 (caused by SARS-CoV-2) are coronaviruses known to target the respiratory system, sometimes leading to severe pneumonia and, potentially, lasting lung damage in the most affected patients.

During the initial outbreak of COVID-19 in China, clinicians and radiologists observed that some patients, especially those with severe cases, developed abnormalities in lung imaging—such as ground-glass opacities and consolidation—consistent with inflammation and, in some cases, subsequent scarring. Chinese pulmonologists and infectious disease experts did warn that, similar to SARS, COVID-19 could leave some survivors with lingering lung damage. However, they also noted that the scale and severity of these aftereffects were still being studied.

The claim that COVID-19 lung scarring is “more severe than SARS 17 years ago” requires careful analysis. SARS affected just over 8,000 people worldwide, but its mortality rate was higher, and survivors did report persistent lung problems, including fibrosis. COVID-19, by contrast, has infected hundreds of millions globally, with a wide spectrum of disease severity. Studies conducted in China and elsewhere have shown that a subset of COVID-19 survivors—particularly those who were hospitalized with severe pneumonia—do exhibit signs of lung scarring months after recovery. Some experts have suggested that, because COVID-19 has affected so many more people, the absolute number of individuals with lung sequelae is higher, although the percentage of survivors developing severe lung fibrosis may be lower compared to SARS.

It is also important to note that the majority of people with mild or moderate COVID-19 do not appear to suffer permanent lung damage. The risk of scarring is greatest among those who required intensive care or mechanical ventilation. Chinese medical experts have called for ongoing monitoring of COVID-19 survivors, especially those with pre-existing health conditions, to assess long-term lung function and intervene where necessary.

In conclusion, the social media post correctly reflects concerns raised by Chinese experts regarding the possibility of lung scarring after COVID-19 infection. While there is evidence that COVID-19 can cause lasting lung damage in some patients, particularly those with severe disease, the assertion that it is categorically “more severe than SARS” is nuanced. The potential for long-term lung effects exists, but the severity and prevalence depend on individual patient factors and the overall scale of the pandemic. The issue remains an important area of ongoing medical research and public health monitoring.

A claim circulating on social media suggests that individuals can test their lungs for COVID-19 at home through a self-check. The post implies that there are simple methods, possibly involving breathing exercises or breath-holding, that can determine if someone has COVID-19 or if their lungs are functioning properly. This article examines the validity of these claims, provides context about COVID-19 testing, and explains the potential dangers of relying on unproven self-checks.

Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, misinformation and unverified health advice have spread widely online. One recurring theme has been the suggestion that people can diagnose or screen themselves for COVID-19 infection by performing at-home breathing tests. Examples include holding one’s breath for a set number of seconds, taking deep breaths without coughing, or other similar breathing exercises. Proponents of these methods suggest that failure or difficulty performing these actions could indicate compromised lung function or a COVID-19 infection.

Medical experts and health authorities have routinely debunked these claims. COVID-19 is a respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. While the virus can cause symptoms such as cough, fever, and shortness of breath, the severity and presence of symptoms vary widely among individuals. Many people infected with the virus experience no symptoms at all, while others may develop mild to severe symptoms, including pneumonia and acute respiratory distress.

The idea that a person can self-diagnose COVID-19 or assess their lung health simply by holding their breath or performing a breathing exercise is not supported by scientific evidence. Breath-holding ability is influenced by many factors, including age, physical fitness, anxiety, and pre-existing lung conditions. A person without COVID-19 may have difficulty holding their breath due to unrelated health issues, while someone with COVID-19—especially in the early stages—may have no difficulty at all. Furthermore, some COVID-19 patients experience “silent hypoxia,” where dangerously low oxygen levels occur without obvious symptoms.

The only reliable way to confirm a COVID-19 infection is through approved diagnostic tests, such as PCR or rapid antigen tests. These tests detect the presence of the virus or its components in the body. Lung function, if a concern, should be assessed by a healthcare professional using validated tools, such as pulse oximeters, spirometry, or clinical examinations.

Relying on social media self-checks for COVID-19 risks providing a false sense of security or unnecessary alarm. Individuals who are concerned about their health, develop symptoms consistent with COVID-19, or have been exposed to someone with the disease should follow public health guidelines, get tested using approved methods, and seek medical advice as appropriate.

In summary, the claim that a person can test their lungs for COVID-19 with a self-check is misleading and not scientifically supported. Accurate diagnosis and assessment require proper testing and professional evaluation, not at-home breathing exercises or unproven self-checks.

Từ khi đại dịch COVID-19 bùng phát, thông tin sai lệch và các lời khuyên sức khỏe chưa được xác minh đã lan truyền rộng rãi trên mạng. Một chủ đề lặp lại là việc khuyến khích người dân tự chẩn đoán hoặc sàng lọc nhiễm virus SARS-CoV-2 tại nhà thông qua các bài kiểm tra hô hấp. Các ví dụ bao gồm việc giữ hơi thở trong một khoảng thời gian nhất định, hít thở sâu mà không ho, hoặc các bài tập hô hấp tương tự. Chuyên gia y tế và các cơ quan y tế đã thường xuyên bác bỏ những tuyên bố này. Bệnh COVID-19 là một bệnh nhiễm trùng đường hô hấp do virus SARS-CoV-2 gây ra. Mặc dù virus có thể gây ra các triệu chứng như ho, sốt và khó thở, nhưng mức độ nghiêm trọng và sự hiện diện của triệu chứng có thể khác nhau tùy theo từng người. Ý tưởng rằng một người có thể tự chẩn đoán nhiễm virus SARS-CoV-2 hoặc đánh giá chức năng phổi chỉ bằng cách giữ hơi thở hoặc thực hiện bài tập hô hấp không được hỗ trợ bởi bằng chứng khoa học. Khả năng giữ hơi thở bị ảnh hưởng bởi nhiều yếu tố, bao gồm tuổi tác, sức khỏe thể chất, lo lắng và các bệnh lý hô hấp sẵn có. Ngoài ra, một số bệnh nhân mắc COVID-19 có thể trải qua "hypoxia không triệu chứng", nơi mức oxy trong máu giảm nguy hiểm nhưng không có triệu chứng rõ rệt.

Phương pháp duy nhất đáng tin cậy để xác nhận nhiễm virus SARS-CoV-2 là các xét nghiệm chẩn đoán được phê duyệt, như xét nghiệm PCR hoặc xét nghiệm kháng nguyên nhanh. Các xét nghiệm này phát hiện sự hiện diện của virus hoặc các thành phần của nó trong cơ thể. Nếu có lo ngại về chức năng phổi, cần được đánh giá bởi chuyên gia y tế sử dụng các công cụ đã được xác minh, như máy đo nồng độ oxy trong máu, xét nghiệm chức năng phổi (spirometry) hoặc khám lâm sàng.

Việc dựa vào các bài kiểm tra tự kiểm trên mạng xã hội để chẩn đoán nhiễm virus SARS-CoV-2 có thể gây ra cảm giác an toàn giả tạo hoặc lo ngại không cần thiết. Những người lo lắng về sức khỏe, xuất hiện các triệu chứng phù hợp với COVID-19 hoặc đã tiếp xúc với người nhiễm bệnh nên tuân thủ các hướng dẫn y tế công cộng, tiến hành xét nghiệm theo phương pháp được chấp thuận và tìm kiếm tư vấn y tế phù hợp.

Tóm lại, tuyên bố rằng người có thể kiểm tra phổi để phát hiện nhiễm virus SARS-CoV-2 thông qua bài kiểm tra tự kiểm là sai lệch và không được hỗ trợ bởi khoa học. Chẩn đoán và đánh giá chính xác đòi hỏi xét nghiệm đúng cách và đánh giá chuyên nghiệp, chứ không phải các bài tập hô hấp tại nhà hoặc các phương pháp tự kiểm chưa được chứng minh.

The rise of digital tools to track and mitigate the spread of COVID-19 has led to the proliferation of various mobile applications, each promising to help users monitor exposure risks and symptoms. Among these is the Away COVID-19 App, which has recently been the subject of criticism on social media, with users questioning its reliability and safety. This article examines these claims, providing context and analysis to assess the validity of concerns surrounding the app.

First, it is important to understand what the Away COVID-19 App purports to do. Designed as a public health tool, the app typically offers features such as exposure notification, symptom tracking, and information on nearby testing locations. The goal of such applications is to promote timely awareness and encourage effective self-isolation or testing when users may have been exposed to the virus.

Reliability concerns about COVID-19 tracking apps are not new. These apps rely heavily on accurate data input, user compliance, and robust technical infrastructure. If an app suffers from frequent bugs, inaccurate notifications, or unreliable updates, users may begin to doubt its efficacy. In the case of the Away COVID-19 App, users have reported issues ranging from delayed exposure alerts to incorrect symptom assessments. Some have noted that the app provides notifications long after potential exposures have occurred, diminishing the usefulness of such alerts. Others have mentioned discrepancies between the app’s recommendations and official local health guidelines.

Safety is another critical issue, particularly in the context of sensitive health information. COVID-19 tracking apps collect and process personal data, including location information, health status, and contact history. If an app lacks strong encryption, transparent privacy policies, or clear user consent mechanisms, the risk of data breaches or misuse increases. Some users have voiced concerns that the Away COVID-19 App does not adequately disclose how it handles user data, nor does it provide sufficient options for users to control or delete their information. Additionally, the app’s permissions may be broader than necessary, raising questions about what data is collected and how it is stored.

Another aspect of safety relates to misinformation. If an app provides unclear or incorrect guidance, users may make decisions that inadvertently increase their risk of contracting or spreading COVID-19. Reports of inconsistent advice and vague notifications from the Away COVID-19 App have fueled skepticism about its effectiveness as a public health tool.

In summary, the core claim that the Away COVID-19 App is unreliable and not safe is supported by user reports of technical glitches, questionable exposure notifications, and data privacy concerns. While the app was developed with the intention of aiding public health efforts, its effectiveness is undermined by technical and ethical shortcomings. Users are advised to review privacy policies carefully, rely on official health guidance, and use digital health tools with caution until reliability and safety can be assured.

A social media post has recently gained traction, claiming that spraying a car key with alcohol can cause a car explosion. The post has sparked concern among vehicle owners, especially as the use of alcohol-based sanitizers and cleaning agents has become common practice in the wake of heightened hygiene awareness.

To assess the validity of this claim, it is important to understand both the properties of alcohol and the mechanics of car key systems. Alcohol, particularly isopropyl or ethyl alcohol, is commonly used as a cleaning agent due to its disinfectant qualities. It is true that alcohol is flammable in certain concentrations and under specific conditions, but does its use on a car key pose a real risk of explosion?

Most modern car keys are composed of plastic and metal components, and some include electronic circuitry, such as key fobs. When alcohol is sprayed onto a key, it generally evaporates within seconds, especially in well-ventilated environments. For a fire or explosion to occur, three elements must be present: a sufficient concentration of flammable vapors, an oxidizing agent (such as air), and an ignition source. In the scenario of spraying a key with alcohol, the quantity applied is typically minimal and the liquid evaporates rapidly, making it highly unlikely to accumulate enough vapor to reach the lower explosive limit required for ignition.

Furthermore, car keys themselves do not contain any elements capable of sparking a fire under normal usage. Even in electronic key fobs, the battery operates at low voltage, which is insufficient to ignite alcohol vapors. The only conceivable way an explosion could occur is if an individual repeatedly doused a key in alcohol, stored it in a sealed, unventilated space to allow vapors to accumulate, and then introduced a strong ignition source. This scenario is far removed from typical cleaning practices and is not supported by any documented incidents.

It is also crucial to differentiate between cleaning a car key and cleaning other parts of a vehicle, such as the ignition system or fuel tank, where flammable vapors may be present. Alcohol-based cleaning products are routinely used on car surfaces and accessories without incident. Manufacturers do advise caution when cleaning electronic devices to avoid damage, but the risk they highlight is generally limited to potential corrosion or malfunction, not explosion.

In summary, the assertion that spraying a car key with alcohol can cause a car explosion is not supported by scientific evidence or safety data. Alcohol, while flammable, does not pose a significant risk when used in small quantities for cleaning purposes, especially when allowed to evaporate. Car keys lack the necessary components to trigger an explosion, and no credible reports support the claim made in the social media post. Vehicle owners can safely clean their car keys with alcohol-based products, provided they follow standard precautions and avoid excessive use. The claim is therefore false and should not cause undue alarm.

A video circulating on social media claims to show a man throwing money into the air at New York City's Times Square as a tribute to his friend who died from COVID-19. The footage has garnered widespread attention and sparked conversations about both the ongoing impact of the pandemic and the nature of public tributes.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to consider several aspects: the video's authenticity, the location and timing, the identity and motivation of the individual involved, and whether the tribute is indeed connected to a COVID-19-related death.

The video in question shows a man standing in the heart of Times Square, surrounded by neon billboards and a moderate crowd. He is seen tossing what appears to be cash into the air, prompting onlookers to scramble for the money. The scene is dramatic and visually striking, matching the description provided in the social media post.

Times Square is a well-known location for public demonstrations and performances, making it a plausible setting for such an event. Analysis of the video’s background confirms the recognizable landmarks, suggesting that the location is indeed Times Square. The video appears to have been taken recently, as evidenced by the presence of summer attire and ongoing construction visible in the background, consistent with current conditions in the area.

A closer look at the man’s actions and statements is necessary to verify the tribute’s context. In the video, the man briefly addresses the crowd, stating, “This is for my friend who lost his life to COVID. Rest in peace.” His words are audible on several versions of the video shared online, lending support to the claim that the act was intended as a tribute. However, verifying the identity of the friend and the circumstances of their death is more challenging. No public records or news articles corroborate the individual’s story at this time, and the man’s identity remains undisclosed.

While the video does appear authentic and the tribute seems sincere, there is limited information available to substantiate all aspects of the claim. The pandemic has tragically claimed millions of lives worldwide, and public tributes, both grand and intimate, have become a common way for people to express grief and solidarity. Throwing money as a symbolic gesture is less traditional, but not unprecedented, especially in a public and highly visible location like Times Square.

In conclusion, the core facts of the social media post are largely accurate: a man did throw money in Times Square, and he stated that it was in tribute to a friend who died from COVID-19. However, due to the lack of verifiable details regarding the deceased friend and the man’s identity, some elements of the story remain unverifiable. The video itself is authentic, and the location is confirmed. While questions persist about the full context, the tribute appears to be genuine and reflects the ongoing emotional impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on individuals and communities.

A social media post has recently gained traction, asserting that “not having side effects after getting COVID-19 vaccination indicates that the immunization is not working.” This claim has generated confusion and concern among individuals who received their vaccine without experiencing noticeable side effects. A closer examination reveals that this statement misrepresents how vaccines work and what post-vaccination responses mean for immunity.

COVID-19 vaccines, like other vaccinations, are designed to train the immune system to recognize and combat the virus that causes the disease. When a person receives a COVID-19 vaccine, their body is exposed to a harmless component or a version of the virus, prompting the immune system to develop a memory of the pathogen. This immune memory enables the body to mount a rapid and effective response if exposed to the real virus in the future.

After vaccination, some people experience side effects such as arm soreness, fatigue, mild fever, headaches, or chills. These side effects are signs that the immune system is responding to the vaccine and are generally short-lived. However, not everyone experiences these reactions, and their absence does not mean the vaccine is ineffective.

Immunologists and health experts emphasize that the presence or absence of side effects is not a reliable indicator of immunity. People’s immune systems vary widely based on age, genetics, underlying health, and other factors, all of which can influence how someone feels after vaccination. Some individuals mount a strong immune response without exhibiting any noticeable symptoms, while others may develop side effects even with a similar level of protection.

The core purpose of the COVID-19 vaccine is to stimulate the production of antibodies and activate immune cells that protect against severe illness and hospitalization. Clinical trials and post-market studies have shown that vaccines confer immunity in most recipients, regardless of whether they experience side effects. In fact, the vast majority of vaccinated individuals develop protective immune responses, as confirmed by laboratory tests measuring antibody levels and other markers of immunity.

It is also important to note that mild side effects are common and expected, but their absence does not mean the body is not responding. Some people simply do not notice minor symptoms, or their immune response does not produce overt signs. The lack of side effects should not be interpreted as a failure of the vaccine.

In summary, the claim that not having side effects after COVID-19 vaccination indicates the immunization is not working is inaccurate. The absence of side effects is a normal outcome for many and does not reflect vaccine efficacy. Individuals who do not experience side effects can be reassured that the vaccine is still likely to provide the intended protection against COVID-19. The key measure of vaccine success is immune protection, not the presence of short-term side effects.

最近、SNSで投稿された「コロナウイルスのワクチンを接種した後、副作用がないということはワクチンが効いていないことを示す」という主張が注目を集めています。この主張は、ワクチンを接種して明らかな副作用を感じなかった人々の間で混乱と懸念を引き起こしています。この声明は、ワクチンの仕組みや接種後の反応が免疫に与える意味を誤解させています。

コロナウイルスのワクチンは、他のワクチンと同様に、免疫系が病原体を認識し、その病気を撲滅するように訓練するためのものです。ワクチンを接種すると、人体は無害な成分や病原体の一部に触れ、免疫系がその病原体の記憶を形成します。この免疫記憶は、今後、実際のウイルスに遭遇した際に迅速かつ効果的な反応を引き起こすようにします。

接種後、一部の人々は腕の痛み、疲労感、軽い発熱、頭痛、寒気などの副作用を感じることがあります。これらの副作用は、免疫系がワクチンに反応していることを示す兆候であり、一般的に短時間で消えます。しかし、すべての人々がこのような反応を経験するわけではなく、副作用がないこと自体がワクチンが効かないことを意味するわけではありません。

免疫学者や医療専門家は、副作用の有無が免疫の有無を示す指標として信頼性が低いと強調しています。人々の免疫系は年齢、遺伝子、基礎疾患などの要因によって大きく異なり、接種後の感覚にも影響を与えます。一部の人々は、明らかにした症状を示さずに強い免疫反応を引き起こす一方、他の人々は、保護レベルが似たような場合でも副作用を感じることがあります。

コロナウイルスワクチンの基本的な目的は、抗体の産生を促進し、重症化や入院を防ぐ免疫細胞を活性化させることです。臨床試験や市販後の研究は、ワクチンがほとんどの受容者に免疫を付与することを示しており、副作用を感じるかどうかに関係なく、ワクチンが効くかどうかはこの免疫の有無で判断されます。実際、検査で抗体レベルや他の免疫指標を測定した結果、ワクチン接種者の中にはほぼすべてが保護的な免疫反応を示しています。

また、軽い副作用は一般的で予想されるものですが、その absence は体が反応していないことを意味しません。一部の人々は、軽い症状に気づかないか、または免疫反応が顕著な症状を引き起こさない場合があります。副作用がないことは、ワクチンの失敗を示すものではありません。

結論として、「コロナウイルスワクチンを接種した後、副作用がないということは、ワクチンが効いていないことを示す」という主張は誤りです。副作用の absence は多くの人々にとって普通の結果であり、ワクチンの効果を示すものではありません。副作用を感じない人々でも、コロナウイルスに対する予定された保護が得られている可能性が高いことを安心して良いでしょう。ワクチンの成功の鍵は免疫保護であり、短期間の副作用の有無ではありません。

article_content:
A recent social media post claims that the Ministry of Public Health has issued a guideline stating, “People should be home isolated if infected.” This statement has garnered significant attention, especially amid ongoing concerns regarding infectious diseases such as COVID-19. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine the context in which such public health guidelines are issued, the specifics of current recommendations from the Ministry, and how these measures are typically implemented.

Home isolation as a recommendation for those infected with contagious illnesses is not a new concept. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Ministry of Public Health, like many health authorities worldwide, adopted home isolation as a strategy to contain the spread of the virus, particularly for patients who exhibited mild or no symptoms. This approach aimed to reduce the burden on healthcare facilities, reserve hospital beds for severe cases, and enable individuals to recover in a familiar environment while minimizing the risk of transmission to others.

Guidelines from the Ministry of Public Health have generally outlined specific circumstances under which home isolation is appropriate. These typically include patients with mild symptoms, those who are not at high risk for severe disease, and individuals who have the means to isolate safely in their homes, meaning they have access to a separate room and can minimize contact with others. The guidelines often detail the duration of isolation, monitoring protocols, and the importance of seeking medical attention if symptoms worsen.

It is also important to note that the Ministry’s recommendations have evolved over time in response to changing epidemiological data, the availability of vaccines, and the strain on healthcare systems. For instance, during periods of high community transmission or hospital overcrowding, home isolation was emphasized as a practical necessity. Conversely, during periods of lower transmission or for certain high-risk groups, more stringent measures, such as hospitalization or supervised isolation, may have been recommended.

As of the most recent updates, the Ministry continues to recommend home isolation for individuals who test positive for certain contagious illnesses, provided they meet the criteria for safe home care. This approach is supplemented by clear instructions on monitoring symptoms, maintaining communication with healthcare providers, and adhering to strict hygiene practices to protect household members.

In summary, the claim that the Ministry of Public Health has issued a guideline advising infected individuals to remain in home isolation is accurate, but with important caveats. The recommendation applies primarily to those with mild symptoms and the capacity to safely isolate at home. The Ministry’s guidelines are nuanced and tailored to the current public health context, emphasizing both individual and community safety. Therefore, while the social media post captures the essence of the Ministry’s current stance, it simplifies the guidance, which in practice is more detailed and conditional.

article_content:
In recent months, a social media post has circulated widely, claiming that “23 people died in Norway after [they] received the COVID-19 vaccine.” The statement has generated concern and confusion, prompting questions about vaccine safety and the context behind these reported deaths. A closer examination reveals a need for nuance and context to fully understand the circumstances surrounding this claim.

The claim refers to events in January 2021, shortly after Norway began its COVID-19 vaccination campaign. Norwegian health authorities reported that 23 elderly individuals died following administration of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine. The majority of these individuals were nursing home residents, many of whom were in frail health and had serious underlying medical conditions prior to vaccination.

Norwegian officials at the time emphasized that, given the high risk of severe outcomes from COVID-19 for elderly populations, nursing home residents were among the first to receive the vaccine. In Norway, more than 400 people typically die each week in nursing homes and long-term care facilities due to various causes. Therefore, when vaccinating this demographic, some deaths occurring shortly after vaccination were to be expected, regardless of vaccine administration.

The Norwegian Medicines Agency and public health authorities investigated these reported deaths. Their analysis concluded that the deaths did not show evidence of being directly caused by the vaccine. However, they did acknowledge that for very frail patients, even mild side effects—such as fever and nausea—could potentially contribute to a decline in health or hasten death in those already near the end of life.

As a result of these findings, Norwegian health officials updated their guidance to recommend that doctors carefully assess extremely frail and terminally ill patients before administering the vaccine. This was a precautionary measure, not an indication that the vaccine itself posed a widespread danger.

International health authorities, including the World Health Organization and the European Medicines Agency, reviewed the Norwegian reports. They reiterated that the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine was safe and effective for the vast majority of people, including elderly populations, and that the benefits of vaccination in preventing COVID-19 far outweighed the risks, even among high-risk groups.

In summary, while it is accurate that 23 elderly individuals in Norway died after receiving the COVID-19 vaccine, the available evidence does not indicate that the vaccine directly caused these deaths. The reports highlight the importance of careful clinical assessment for the most vulnerable patients before vaccination but do not undermine the overall safety profile of COVID-19 vaccines. Public health authorities continue to monitor vaccine safety closely and update recommendations as new data emerge.
